Manchester City face possible points deductions, expulsion, financial penalties or the stripping of their titles. It is unclear when the decision on what the punishment will be will come, especially given that City are expected to appeal.
The outcome also has significant impacts for the Premier League. In taking on one of its biggest clubs, having successfully punished two smaller ones, they risk appearing toothless. Certainly the eyes of European football will be on them as the impact of the decision will put the integrity of the competition into focus.
It may also see more English fans call for a model like the 50+1 rule to be integrated. Some voices were raised in England after the Saudi sovereign wealth fund PIF took over Premier League club Newcastle United in 2021 , and others continued during the attempted establishment of a European Super League in 2021 .

title: Diesel prices are surging putting further pressure on Europe
description: Trucks, farms and industry are powered with diesel. Now prices are soaring due to refinery disruptions, supply shortages and geopolitical tensions. A potential US export ban could make Europe's diesel crunch even worse.
content:
Even if you don't fill your own vehicle with diesel, its price has a big impact on your life.
While gasoline is mainly a consumer fuel for cars, diesel powers much of the wider economy, from freight transport and farming equipment to construction and industry.
That is why diesel shortages or price shocks can have a bigger economic impact than higher gasoline prices by raising the cost of moving goods and operating heavy machinery.
As businesses become strained, these higher energy costs will be passed on to consumers and add to a growing cost-of-living crisis and inflation . So what's driving global diesel prices higher?
The United States and China are among the world's largest diesel producers. China keeps much of it for domestic use, leaving the US as the world's biggest diesel exporter.
Still, the weekly average price of a gallon of diesel is now $6.52 (€5.73) in the country, according to the US Energy Information Administration , a big increase from a year ago when it averaged $3.74 per gallon or two years ago when it averaged $3.53 a gallon.
President Donald Trump recently called on Ukraine's president to stop targeting oil refineries in Russia "because he's causing a shortage of diesel."
Russia is one of the world's other biggest diesel suppliers. But since 2022, some of its oil refineries have been attacked as many as 15 times , according to the International Energy Agency.
The agency estimates that diesel production in Russia is down by nearly 30% from 2025 levels. Moscow has now restricted diesel exports to protect domestic supplies.
As Russian production declined, the US went into high gear to help make up the difference, but even this was not enough. And on September 22, Trump announced that his administration was also considering a diesel export ban.
Such a move is likely an attempt to bring down domestic prices ahead of the November midterm elections since energy prices and affordability have become important campaign issues.
Leading energy lobby groups have come out against such a plan, and many industry experts think a ban would be slow to bring down prices or could backfire by pushing US refiners to reduce production, push up prices, or both.
For Europe, more expensive diesel could have dramatic consequences.
"Decades of policy incentives, such as tax advantages, left Europe's vehicle fleet far more diesel-heavy than regions like the US," said Georg Zachmann, a senior fellow at Brussels-based Bruegel think tank.
"As a result, the EU is structurally long on gasoline, which it exports, and short on diesel, which it must import," added Zachmann, who specializes in energy and climate policies.
In the EU, just over 38% of passenger cars are diesel and road transport, including freight, makes up 77% of total diesel and gas oil consumption, according to a briefing published by Transport & Environment, a Brussels-based advocacy group.
This reliance on diesel-powered transport "leaves drivers and businesses particularly exposed to oil and fuel price shocks," wrote Juliette Egal, the briefing's lead author.
The NGO calculated that EU drivers are paying €30 more for a 50-liter tank of diesel on average since the start of the war in Iran . An average German long-haul truck driver is paying an extra €236 a week.
Increased fuel costs for EU road transport add up to €270 million a day — of that, €203 million is for diesel, according to the briefing. Overall, the EU economy has seen additional costs of €40 billion from road diesel since the beginning of the war.
In the near term, Russia's crude oil processing volumes are the single fastest-moving lever, said Skip York, a nonresident fellow at Rice University's Center for Energy Studies in Houston, Texas.
"Each new wave of Ukrainian strikes shows up in diesel prices within days, unlike Hormuz, which has been running at a depressed but relatively stable flow rate for months," he added.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
York points out that, perhaps surprisingly, crude oil production, the raw material needed to make diesel and gasoline, isn't the biggest constraint. That is why oil prices have moved modestly while diesel has soared.
"The oil bottleneck has shifted from 'not enough crude' in March/April to 'not enough refining capacity' since August," the expert told DW.
Now refinery disruptions matter most, he said, because "both the Ukraine drone campaign and the Hormuz conflict are knocking out working refining capacity faster than anyone can replace it."
Still, the Strait of Hormuz "is the bigger structural risk" for diesel prices in the long term.
Globally, refinery capacity has "dropped substantially, and diesel is particularly affected," agreed Zachmann.
Prolonged fighting in the Middle East or Russia could add to the problems for Europe and other diesel users. US export restrictions could make this situation even worse.
US diesel exports to Europe are up around 37% since last year and now account for about 8% of European demand, says York. This makes the country an important alternative to diesel from Russia and the Persian Gulf.
If the US blocks exports, it would be a big shock and mean even higher diesel prices, said Zachmann. The question is whether the EU would retaliate and export less gasoline to the US "making both sides worse off" by pushing up both US gasoline prices and EU diesel prices.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Additionally, winter is just around the corner for the Northern Hemisphere. Refineries may struggle to meet demand for both heating oil and diesel, further tightening supplies.
A wave of refinery closures in Europe and the US since 2019 has made the diesel market vulnerable, said York, and this has hit the buffer of spare refining capacity that used to absorb shocks.
"Essentially, the market has fewer 'extra barrels' standing by," he underscored. "So, the loss of any barrel hits supply much more directly than it used to."

title: Will Jürgen Klopp's charisma be enough for Germany?
description: After defeat to Greece, Jürgen Klopp faces the first real test of his tenure as coach of Germany's national men's football team. Can his charisma alone push this group forward?
content:
In his first season in charge at Liverpool , Jürgen Klopp lost just one of his first five games.
Germany hopes for a similar run emerges after a shock 1-0 defeat to Greece, a team that hasn't qualified for a major international tournament in 12 years. The defeat left Klopp with just one point after his first two games in charge of the national team.
True to form, the head coach took responsibility for the loss, shielding this new crop of Germany players from criticism.
"We have been together for a week now, all mixed together, and that needs time," Klopp said after the match.
"Let the new players develop. The established players are top players at their clubs, and they have my support. Feel free to criticize me, but not the boys. We don't need to completely tear everything apart. I was surprised that some people booed. The future is as bright as we make it. We'll take it on with everything we have."
He also emphasized development over short-term panic, citing the need for more training sessions to cement the automatic responses needed to break down well-organized defenses.
Herein lies the challenge for one of football's greatest coaches. In likely his final job as a head coach, can the multiple league winner adapt his coaching methods to work in the national team? Klopp, a coach and a person famous for his ability to develop relationships and grow a team at a club, has said he believes he can adapt.
His legacy at Borussia Dortmund and Liverpool leaves no doubt that his communication style is what this team needs. His charismatic focus on developing a culture and growing collectively in connection with the fans is what is required.
After many years of frustration and pain watching Germany's men at major tournaments, the biggest mistake would be to tear down this new group before it even begins.
The team both needs and deserves the time to figure out how far it can go. Bambase Conte and Hennes Behrens made their debuts against Greece after a host of others had done so against the Netherlands .
These are the first steps towards finding out who will drive Germany towards an improved outing at the 2028 European Championship. It is the main reason why Klopp chose so many players for these first four games .
But what if, for all of Klopp's positivity and culture building , this new generation of German players is just not good enough to win a trophy? Clearly, it is too soon to know the answer, as Klopp himself has said.
"We want to help prepare these players to be competing at the very top over the next two or three years," Klopp had said at his unveiling.
"We took a different approach and focused not on what we don't have, but on what we do have."
What Germany has right now is both a new team looking to grow and a team that just suffered their first-ever defeat to Greece.
At Liverpool, it took Jürgen Klopp two years and approximately 500 training sessions to reach the point where the team looked like his. In the 2017-18 season, they reached the Champions League final . Alongside the time it took for the team to learn the new system, new signings, notably Mohamed Salah, Roberto Firmino and Sadio Mane, improved the quality.
Klopp doesn't have that option with the German national team. He has to do more with fewer training sessions — Klopp will have approximately 200 before Euro 2028. The closest he can get to new signings is by calling up uncapped Germany players — there were 11 first-time call-ups in this Germany squad.
The 59-year-old said his whole career brought him to this job . It might well prove to be the greatest challenge of his career, too.

title: Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in Nations League match overshadowed by political controversy
description: Ireland easily beat Israel in a Nations League fixture that 24 hours earlier appeared in doubt. One Irish player pulled out of the match to express his opposition to Israel's actions in the Gaza Strip.
content:
The Irish team bowed their heads during playing of the Israeli national anthem on Sunday night and they declined to shake hands with their opponents, a gesture that is customary before international fixtures.
Ireland played the match wearing black armbands in memory of those killed in Israel's military operation in the Gaza Strip , and just 24 hours earlier it was unclear whether the match would go ahead at all.
On Saturday, the players voted in favor of playing what was technically a home match for Israel in Debrecen, Hungary , despite widespread opposition to their participation among the Irish public.
David Courell, the chief executive of the Irish FA (FAI), told a press conference that had been delayed for several hours while players and coaches met to discuss the issue, that a significant majority of the squad had voted to play.
"Based on that, the association took ⁠the decision on behalf of Irish ​football that this fixture would continue, as we have always intended to fulfil the fixtures," he said.
However, the vote was not unanimous and one player, reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, decided to pull out of the squad for this and a second match against Israel during this international break.
In Sunday's match, Troy Parrott netted the opener for Ireland in the 14th minute, with ​Adam Idah scoring two minutes later. Jack Moylan added a third in the 25th to make the final score 3-0.
The fixture was played in a largely empty stadium in Debrecen , with just a few hundred Israeli fans and a handful of Irish supporters in attendance.
The FAI had not reserved any tickets for their fans to attend the match and public broadcaster RTE showed the match without the usual halftime analysis.
Over the previous few days, the Irish team had been under intense pressure from Irish fans and politicians to boycott the fixture.
Ireland has long been a strong supporter of the Palestinian cause and formally recognized a Palestinian state in 2024 alongside Spain and Norway. Dublin has also repeatedly criticized Israel over the Gaza conflict.
A Hamas raid into Israel on October 7, 2023, killed around 1,200 people, prompting Israel's attack on Gaza which has killed over 73,000.
Ireland's next Nations League match was originally scheduled to be played in Dublin on October 4, but due to security concerns, it has been moved to the Serbian town of Backa Topola, where it is to be played behind closed doors.

title: What would Francis of Assisi make of his fame today?
description: The Catholic saint renounced wealth and fame to become a mendicant friar. Yet throughout history, his teachings and life have inspired popes, Dante and even Mussolini.
content:
One could safely say that Francis of Assisi's life — and afterlife — is defined by paradox.
He embraced poverty, yet lies entombed today in a grand basilica in his native Assisi, Italy, with frescoes by renowned medieval artists.
He advocated meekness, yet hundreds of thousands venerated his remains when they went on public display earlier this year to commemorate 800 years since his death on October 3, 1226.
So, why has this Catholic saint inspired papal encyclicals , ecological activism, global pet‑blessing rituals and even the propaganda of former Italian fascist leader Benito Mussolini? And what might Francis make of this fame that he'd shunned while alive?
Born in Assisi, a hill town in central Italy, in 1181 or 1182, he was first named Giovanni di Pietro di Bernardone. His father, a cloth merchant with trade links to France, renamed him Francesco.
Early Franciscan hagiographers, that is medieval writers who recorded his life and shaped how later generations understood him, describe him as a lively, sociable young man who enjoyed singing, parties and the privileges of wealth.
However, he didn't want to join his father's trade; he dreamed of becoming a knight.
In 1202, Francis joined Assisi's forces in a battle against neighboring Perugia. He was captured, spent a year in prison and returned home shaken and ill. This, and a series of subsequent events, precipitated a slow shift in his outlook.
One occurred at the small, ruined Church of San Damiano outside Assisi, where Francis believed he heard Jesus Christ calling on him to "rebuild my church." Taking it literally, he began repairing local chapels. When he ran out of money, he sold cloth from his father's shop, which enraged the latter and led to a dramatic episode in Assisi's town square.
Before the bishop and gathered townspeople, Francis stripped off his fine clothes, renouncing his father, his inheritance and all material comforts. He committed himself to a life of poverty, humility, care for the poor and sick and a deep kinship with nature.
As a wandering preacher, he drew followers and eventually founded the Order of Friars Minor, known today as the Franciscans.
Widely considered the first saint to have miraculously received the stigmata — physical wounds resembling those on the crucified body of Jesus Christ — Francis was canonized by Pope Gregory IX on July 16, 1228. This unusually swift recognition amplified his fame beyond Assisi.
In the following centuries, Francis became one of the most frequently depicted saints in Western art, inspiring works from Dante's "Divine Comedy" to films, children's books and even a 1980 Marvel comic.
"Most saints are seen as unapproachable or unrelatable, but Francis' story of lifelong conversion and the desire to be in a positive relationship with others, God and the rest of creation speaks to people across time and cultures," theologian and former Franciscan friar Daniel P. Horan tells DW.
According to cultural historian Amanda Minervini, this broad appeal is also what made Francis so adaptable across eras.
"In Francis, there seems to be something for everyone: the pacifist, the ascetic, the mason, the environmentalist, the minimalist, the lover of animals also loved by animals, the diplomat, the mystic, the radical, the performer, and even the model of a different kind of masculinity," they tell DW.
Minervini points out that his image has been reconstructed throughout history . Their research highlights one particularly jarring example: Francis' political appropriation by Benito Mussolini's fascist regime.
In their recent book, "St. Francis and Mussolini: Fascist Appropriations of a Beloved Italian Saint" (2026), they explain how fascist rhetoric manipulated Francis' stigmata, reframing them as symbols of heroic suffering and sacrifice. "The wounds of the saint were thus invoked to glorify sacrifice and inspire Italian youth to go to war."
Noting how Mussolini chose to be symbolically baptized in 1927 to strengthen his alliance with the Vatican , they add, "St. Francis offered a particularly useful means of conferring religious legitimacy upon political power."
Minervini's research shows that Francis' pacifism, "likely because he had known what war meant," was deliberately played down. Their book reproduces a confidential note addressed to military chaplains in 1929, which expressed concern that they might preach ideals of peace to the troops.
"This document provides clear evidence that peace was an aspect of Francesco's legacy that fascist groups sought to suppress rather than promote."
Furthermore, after Italy — a former Axis power along with Nazi Germany — switched sides and joined the Allies during World War II, the latter were often willing to condone or overlook Italy's crimes rather than investigate its fascist past.
"In this climate, many fascists remained in place, and the politically compromised image of Francis was quietly set aside," explains Minervini.
Francis has, however, remained associated with peace-making.
In 1219, during the Fifth Crusade , he traveled with the crusading army to Damietta, a port city in northern Egypt and obtained permission to cross into the Muslim camp and meet personally with the sultan, Malik al-Kamil. He aimed to convert the sultan and end the bloody conflict.
Describing his action as "an extraordinarily audacious thing to do," Minervini says the encounter did not produce the conversion or political breakthrough Francis may have hoped for, but his unscathed return ensured early sources took notice of him.
Horan, the former Franciscan friar, adds that despite Christians viewing Muslims as the enemy back then, St. Francis "would not go along with that dehumanizing perspective" and instead celebrated "the shared humanity and brotherhood he recognized in the Sultan."
But he is most widely known as an animal lover and an early figure of environmental consciousness.
"He was ahead of his time both theologically and in terms of modern natural sciences, recognizing the complexity of the cosmos and the fact that human beings are also creatures in relationship with the world around us," says Horan, author of "Francis of Assisi and the Future of Faith" (2012).
In 1979, Pope John Paul II declared Francis the patron saint of ecology, while the Argentinian Jorge Mario Bergoglio chose the saint as his papal namesake when he became Pope Francis in 2013.
This pope would later publish "Laudato Si'" in 2015 — based on the saint's 1225 hymn "Canticle of the Creatures," in which he addresses natural elements as "Brother Sun," "Sister Moon" and "Sister Mother Earth."
The pope's encyclical connected environmental destruction directly to human suffering, besides critiquing consumerism and the "throwaway culture," and urging humanity to undergo an "ecological conversion."
"I also believe that in a time of deep polarization and economic inequality that St Francis models another way of being in the world, one that prioritizes relationship and community over individual gain and power," says Horan.
"It's always tricky to try and guess what St. Francis, who died 800 years ago this October, would think about anything today. Our world is so unlike his own. But we do know that in his own time he was very uncomfortable with the positive reception he and his brother friars were receiving across Europe," says Horan.
Minervini suggests that he might have been more comfortable with representations of himself as a pacifist saint.
"I suspect he would be profoundly troubled, perhaps even furious, as it is known he could get upset, by the condition of our late-capitalist, technocratic world and by the ways in which we continue to understand ourselves as separate from, and superior to, the other creatures."

title: Backlash over data centers tests Europe's AI ambitions
description: Massive data centers needed to run AI are triggering protests across Europe. Their operators counter that they boost digital sovereignty and energy independence.
content:
Like coal-fired power plants and wind turbines, few people actually want a data center in their backyard. But they do want to use their services. As a global debate rages about the potential dangers of artificial intelligence, there are also many local discussions about where exactly the data centers needed to train and run AI should be built.
This is currently a major issue in Europe, where many governments and companies have decided that they would prefer to store data in Europe rather than in the United States, which is the global leader in computing. But more digital sovereignty in Europe will mean more consumption of the continent's resources.
According to the German Ministry for Economic Affairs, for every kilowatt-hour of electricity consumed, an average of between 0.4 and 4.4 liters (0.8 and 9.3 pints) of water is used to cool data centers , with the water either evaporating or being diverted back to tanks in a warmed state.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The summer that just ended was the hottest on record in Europe — in some areas, water use was restricted for residents, agriculture and even nuclear power plants. The summers are expected to get warmer, so many are wondering about the potential water consumption of data centers in the future.
They are also worried about the high electricity consumption of the centers. Fingrid, Finland's national grid operator, recently forecast that electricity consumption would rise by almost 40% if all projects with signed connection agreements were implemented in full.
This week, the European Commission announced a new scheme for data centers to increase transparency on their energy and water use. Those with a capacity of more than 500 kW will receive an efficiency grade that will also take into account their contribution to the grid, such as the reuse of waste heat. "Tripling our data center capacity cannot mean tripling the pressure on our grids, our water and our energy bills," said Teresa Ribera, the Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for a Clean, Just and Competitive Transition.
Europe's most powerful data centers have primarily been built near the major cities of Frankfurt, London , Amsterdam, Paris and Dublin (FLAP-D) because of high connectivity, proximity to users and businesses, and well-established ecosystems with specialized engineers and secure supply chains.
However, according to a report by the investment group CBRE, the situation is changing as these markets face power and grid infrastructure constraints. New data centers are being built in the Dutch city of Groningen, Barcelona in Spain or the Belgian capital Brussels, as well as in more rural areas.
And as this happens, there are more and more protests taking place, both on and offline. Earlier this month, hundreds turned up for a protest in front of tech giant Google's offices in the Austrian city of Linz, demonstrating against its already advanced plans to build a data center in the small town of Kronstorf.
Earlier this month, bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney successfully led a campaign to overturn planning permission for a proposed data center in the village of Killala, arguing that it would breach national climate policy.
In central France, meanwhile, several elected officials in the village of Etrechet have resigned over Google's plans to build a massive data center, which, at full capacity, would require between 880 megawatts and 1.1 gigawatts of electricity or the equivalent of the total output of a nuclear power plant. Etrechet mayor Florence Laurent told the French daily Le Monde that she was resigning out of a "sense of powerlessness, since the village has no decision-making power" regarding the project.
Some operators of data centers argue that the facilities can be built in such a way that they save energy . A large data center currently being built in Marseille will reportedly use a cooling system that requires 30% less power and consumes no water.
Other data centers, in Scandinavia, for example, use waste heat from the servers and route it into district heating networks via heat exchangers and pumps.
This spring, the German energy company E.ON published the results of a survey that found nearly three-quarters of people would be more likely to welcome data centers near residential areas if they fed their waste heat into the heating network.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Data center operators also argue that the facilities can serve the public by connecting the batteries that usually provide backup power to local grids so that there is uninterrupted service in the event of power outages or at times of peak demand.
For proponents of building more data centers in Europe, the facilities not only contribute to the continent's digital sovereignty but also help to strengthen energy independence.
Monir Ghaedi contributed to this article, which was translated from German.

title: Bundesliga, other top European leagues call for major FIFA reforms
description: The Bundesliga and three other leading European football leagues have said major reforms to world-governing body FIFA are "essential." However, they stopped short of calling for the resignation of boss Gianni Infantino.
content:
The letter released this Friday and signed by the heads of the Bundesliga, the Premier League, La Liga and Serie A called for major changes to how FIFA operates — and for a greater say in decision-making.
"Football's ​longstanding foundations have, in recent years, been threatened by a fundamental governance problem, whereby FIFA's president has actively promoted exploitative ​ideas rather than safeguarding against them," it said.
FIFA President Gianni Infantino has been facing a wave of criticism since late July, when his plan for private investment through a commercial vehicle, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), emerged. The idea was for FFE to organize FIFA's tournaments while maximizing profits.
Vigorous opposition from UEFA, European football's governing body, as well as CONCACAF (North and Central America plus the Caribbean) and the Asian Football Confederation led Infantino to quickly drop the plan.
However, the league bosses noted that this had not solved a deeper problem and appeared to dismiss a recent announcement by Infantino of an independent external review of FIFA governance as well as consultations on strengthening decision-making processes.
"It is not enough for surface-level, process changes to be explored in the aftermath of FFE — fundamental governance reform is essential to restore clear constitutional boundaries within FIFA, including confidence that individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference," Friday's letter from the leagues said.
The last line was in reference to the widespread discontent around FIFA's handling of the Folarin Balogun case, with the United States striker's one-match ban being suspended to allow him to play a World Cup last-16 match against Belgium in July. While the ban was imposed by FIFA's disciplinary committee, it came after US President Donald Trump had personally called Infantino asking for a "review" of the ban — something Trump publicly admitted.
The leagues on Friday called for greater checks and balances to be implemented at FIFA, while at the same time demanding that they and others be given a say in decisions such as increases in the number of international matches.
The letter went on to say that "… when FIFA takes major unilateral decisions directly affecting us — for example, by expanding the International Match Calendar (IMC) and extending the periods in which domestic competitions must pause — the stakeholders most affected are not meaningfully involved in the decision-making process.
"A FIFA governance that concentrates unchecked regulatory, commercial and political power in a single office, while relegating affected stakeholders to mere advisory status, is not fit for purpose."
The letter, while implying much criticism of Infantino, did not call for him to step down 3 it didn't even mention him by name.
The letter comes as UEFA has said it is looking for a suitable candidate to challenge Infantino in the next presidential election in March, in which Infantino has said he will run for reelection.
UEFA has also called for an independent external review of how the FFE plan was developed, and has filed legal applications through the US courts for the disclosure of documents related to the plan. This was with a view to a possible criminal complaint being lodged in Switzerland if it is established that Infantino undervalued FFE at $20 billion (€17.5 billion).
FIFA has described UEFA's legal moves as a "smear campaign" against it but has not yet commented on Friday's letter from the league bosses.
Infantino aims to discuss his proposals at a FIFA Council meeting in Zurich on October 15, a week after UEFA is to hold a meeting of all of its 55 member associations on October 8 in Berlin.
Any person aiming to challenge Infantino in the March 18, 2027 FIFA presidential election must register as a candidate by November 18.

title: Jürgen Klopp starts Germany job with shaky Netherlands draw
description: A late Netherlands goal denied Jürgen Klopp a win in his first match as Germany coach. The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund boss has big ambitions, but the game showed he's going to need more time to achieve them.
content:
It looked, until the final moments, as though Germany would somehow hold on and grant Jürgen Klopp a victory in his first game as Germany coach.
"It felt mostly good," Klopp told German broadcaster RTL after the match, with his voice strained after a typically energetic display on the sidelines. "That was really exhausting for both teams today." He added that he naturally wanted a win but that he can "live with the point, too."
In the end, an injury time Cody Gakpo goal meant Klopp and his team had to settle for a 1-1 draw in their Nations League opener against the Netherlands . While the timing of the equalizer will sting, Germany was second best for much of the contest, which turned a ill-tempered at times. Nevertheless, Klopp was upbeat.
"I was very, very, very satisfied with many of the individual performances," he said, before admitting that "we can play better football and create more chances — that's for sure."
Gakpo plays his club football for Liverpool, where Klopp coached for more than eight years . So too does Dutch captain Virgil van Dijk, who thought he'd opened the scoring for the hosts early on, only to see his headed goal ruled out. A close-range finish from Lukas Nmecha then gave Germany the lead but not control of the game.
While there were a few patches of attacking play that resembled the kind of high-intensity, exhilarating football that Klopp produced at Liverpool and, before that, at Borussia Dortmund, Germany looked shaky at the back and were thankful for some wasteful Dutch finishing.
It is, though, difficult to judge much at this early stage. Klopp replaced Julian Nagelsmann after another poor World Cup showing from Germany and, after naming two different squads for the four Nations Leagues games in an extended international period, is still assessing how to make the most of what he has. Three players — Younes Ebnoutalib , Yannik Engelhardt and Philipp Treu — made debuts on Thursday, and more are likely follow over the next three games.
"I won't promise anything [in terms of trophies]. What I can promise is that we will definitely give it a try," he told reporters ahead of the game. "There's an impression that we have less quality than other countries. When things aren't working, you take a closer look and try to bring about changes. That's what we're working on now."
After Germany lost Kai Havertz to injury in the first half, having already had to change to starting XI after Jamal Musiala pulled out of the match in the warmup, the team was left without much of their attacking experience and class.
But Klopp won't panic. His methods, both tactically and emotionally, will take time to bear fruit. At Liverpool, it took nearly five years to win a trophy; at Dortmund, it took three.
"When the system isn't yet in place and the processes aren't yet established, then something like this happens," he said about Wednesday's performance. "I was very pleased with the passion, the intensity, but we can definitely play better."
Usually, waiting for success would not be acceptable for German national team fans. But after repeated recent failures, and with Klopp a popular figure, he has more credit in that bank than his predecessor, Julian Nagelsmann. The last coach to win a World Cup for Germany, Joachim Löw, said he will need it.
"It is crucial now to give him the necessary time and space to implement his ideas," he told the Münchner Merkur/tz newspaper. "Jürgen stands for energy, intensity and a strong bond between the team and the fans. But even for him, not everything will work from one day to the next. After a disappointing World Cup , it takes trust, patience and a team that once again plays for Germany with great conviction."
Klopp has already tried to unite the country behind the team. On the touchline in Amsterdam, he ran through his familiar repertoire of fist bumps, beaming smiles and growls at officials in a cap emblazoned with the words "one of 83 million" on it.
The headgear has already become a familiar sight. It's a reference to Germany's population and the 59-year-old has also referenced the importance of his team, and their flag , as a symbol of nationhood at a time when the far-right AfD (Alternative for Germany) are making substantial electoral gains.
"I'd like to reclaim the flag for myself — or for us," Klopp said. "I want us to always wave it in a way that makes no one think: 'What's wrong with you?' But, rather, that people simply get the feeling that you're happy and understand how lucky you are to have been born, raised or moved to this wonderful country."
While Klopp's charisma makes such a lofty ambition seem somewhat feasible, he's also pragmatic enough to know that for the German national team to be universally loved, it needs to win. Augsburg on Saturday, against Greece in the Nations League, would be a good place to start.

title: Political psychology: Why extremist parties are thriving and what democratic politicians can do against it
description: Far-right and far-left parties are celebrating success after success, leaving moderate politicians in the dust and worrying many Germans. Political psychology helps us understand what's behind growing polarization.
content:
On September 6, Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt held elections for its state parliament. The big winner: The right-wing AfD (Alternative for Germany) party, which garnered 43.8% of the votes; more than ever before.
It's still unclear who will govern the state because the AfD does not have an absolute majority.
But it was a landslide win for the AfD , whose Saxony-Anhalt branch is classified as right-wing extremist by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, and that worries many Germans.
The day after the election, Chancellor Friedrich Merz from the conservative CDU said he was "deeply shocked" by the election results. "Not only did something change in Saxony-Anhalt yesterday but throughout all of Germany."
Merz's CDU lost more than half its share of the ballot compared to the last state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The CDU dropped from 37.1% in 2021 to 17.2% in 2026.
Two weeks later, at state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on September 20, the CDU didn't even make the 5% threshold to enter parliament.
It was the first time ever for the CDU; they got only 4.9% of the vote in the northeastern state. The strongest party was once again the AfD with 38.2%.
That same day, in the city state of Berlin , the socialist Left Party won the election and will likely govern Germany's capital. In Berlin, the CDU was the second-strongest party and the AfD came in third.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
These state elections show that parties on the extreme ends of the political spectrum are growing stronger in Germany.
The country has experience with both extreme right- and left-wing governments: the Nazis that led Germany into World War II and the Socialist Unity Party (SED) that ruled then- East Germany from 1949 until 1989.
A return to extreme politics is a scary proposition for some people.
In a representative monthly survey called "What worries the world?" , the polling institute Ipsos found that almost one-fifth of Germans (18%) said they were worried by growing extremism in the country when they asked about 1,000 people between the ages of 16 and 74 years in March and April 2026.
Generally, people in Germany are concerned about where their country is going. In the Ipsos survey, 82% said they saw Germany as moving in the wrong direction.
Asking people about their fears or worries is just one way to take the nation's temperature. There are other options to measure politically relevant emotions in the population as well.
Kerstin Pahl, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin, told DW that possibilities include quantitative and qualitative surveys, as well as analyzing online discourse and the content people share on social media. It's also possible to read a nation's sentiment by observing real-life displays of emotions, like public protests and demonstrations.
For researchers like Pahl, it's also interesting to see how political issues can come to symbolize much more than their material or factual meaning.
"People may see their region's ailing infrastructure not just as proof of a lack of investment, but also as a sign that they have been forgotten [by their leaders]," said Pahl.
Extremist parties winning a higher percentage of the votes is what we see on the surface. Below that lie two kinds of societal polarization: Affective and ideological polarization.
"Affective polarization is a growing hatred for the political opponent. Most studies investigated this in the context of the US between supporters of the Democrat and the Republican Party ," Eva Walther, head of the social psychology department at the University of Trier in western Germany, told DW. "When this happens on the party level, it's a problem."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Politicians of different parties often have to work together and reach compromises. They don't need to like each other, but they should treat each other with respect, Walther said.
"When this respectful attitude starts crumbling, it's a problem for democracy," she added.
The other phenomenon, ideological polarization, is when society is split into distinct groups based on what issues people view as the most pressing problem for them.
For example, many people to the right of the political center in Germany see migration as the biggest problem, while many people to the left of the political center say it's the climate crisis .
When different crisis situations occur at the same time, such as migration and climate change, researchers refer to a "polycrisis."
Polycrises intensify ideological polarization, making it even harder for societies to find a common way forward.
"At the moment, we have the climate crisis overlapping with an affordable energy crisis , more of an economic problem," Walther said.
In the eyes of those for whom the climate crisis is the most urgent issue, fossil fuels should be abandoned as soon as possible. But for those most concerned with affordable energy, relying only on renewable energy sources would needlessly raise prices.
The belief that a politician is competent and willing to tackle major challenges, to act, is a big factor in how much people trust democracy.
But that's also what makes overlapping crises so hard to manage: No matter which problems politicians attempt to solve first, one part of the population will be disappointed.
"Polycrises make it difficult for politicians to act, which means that people have less trust that politicians can solve the problems important to them," Walther said.
Right-wing extremist parties, however, aim to "satisfy people by giving them simplified answers to complex problems," added Walther.
This leads people to believe that extremist politicians can solve their problems ― which in turn leads to growing polarization.
But politicians from democratic parties can learn from clinical research to tackle this dilemma, according to Walther.
"When a person is in pain and goes to see a doctor, it's important that the doctor recognizes the patient's pain," she said.
Even if the doctor can't instantly solve the issue and make the pain go away, showing that they take the issue and the patient seriously is crucial. And the same goes for politicians.
"They need to make people's needs the first priority in their daily work," Walther said. "People want to be seen, so it's important for politicians to make it clear that they see and understand their problems."
Whether it's a doctor failing a patient or politicians failing the electorate, patient and electorate are likely to scream — and that's a signal we can all read.

title: Could flattering AI make humanity turn on itself?
description: A study shows chatbots mirror users' politics, part of a broader tendency known as AI sycophancy. Researchers fear this could deepen polarization.
content:
A recent wave of headline-grabbing warnings from AI luminaries has fueled fears the technology could escape human control and wipe out humanity. But before artificial intelligence (AI) turns on humanity, it could contribute to humans turning on one another.
Researchers at Brazil 's State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) found that popular chatbots shifted their answers when prompted with hypothetical users' political views. The scientists warn that users could mistake this tailored agreement for an independent assessment, potentially deepening polarization.
In their study published in the journal Scientific Reports , the UNICAMP team tested 21 large language models from developers including OpenAI , Meta , Google , xAI, DeepSeek and Microsoft . The models rated their agreement with 112 statements covering seven areas of Brazilian politics, including the economy, public safety, welfare, corruption and the environment.
Each was tested under three conditions: with no information about the user's politics, with a prompt describing a left-leaning user and with one describing a right-leaning user.
When no information about the user's ideology was given, 20 of the 21 models produced answers that fell on the left of the researchers' political scale, although several were close to the center. Grok 4.1 was the only model that fell on the right.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
When information was provided, every model shifted its answers toward the political orientation described in the prompt.
"The most striking finding was how widespread this behavior was," study co-author Zanoni Dias, a UNICAMP computer scientist, told DW. "All 21 models we evaluated shifted their expressed positions toward the user's stated political orientation, although the magnitude varied substantially."
The researchers described the models as "ideological chameleons" and developed a "chameleon index" measuring how far each shifted.
Meta's Llama 3.1 8B and DeepSeek V3.2 changed their responses least. Google's Gemma 3 27B and OpenAI's GPT-5 Nano showed some of the largest shifts.
Adapting an answer to its audience is not inherently problematic. A chatbot might change its vocabulary, examples or level of detail depending on the user.
But the models changed more than their language or tone: Their political positions shifted.
"The key distinction is between adapting how an answer is communicated and changing the substantive judgment being expressed," Dias said.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"We did not instruct the models to agree with the user or to answer as a partisan representative. Nevertheless, their judgments shifted toward the user's side."
The researchers interpret this as political sycophancy: AI systems reflecting what users appear to want to hear.
A possible explanation is that chatbots are trained to favor answers human evaluators rate highly. If agreeable answers get better ratings, models may learn to echo users' views.
Social media can reinforce beliefs by repeatedly recommending algorithmic content, but a chatbot could go even further. It could create a more personalized echo chamber, generating arguments for a particular user, answering their objections and refining its case throughout the conversation.
Yet users may mistake these tailored responses for impartial analysis, unaware that what a chatbot knows about them may shape its responses.
"The concern is that the same system could validate opposing political positions for different users, with each person interpreting that validation as an independent assessment," Dias said.
Research by Stanford University behavioral scientist Zakary Tormala suggests people may be particularly receptive to arguments they believe came from AI.
"People tend to see AI as more informative, more objective, less biased and less interested in persuading them than another person would be," Tormala told DW. "This can lower people's defenses and make them more receptive to hearing out what AI has to say."
That trust could make political flattery more influential.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"Hearing their own views validated by others is well known to increase people's certainty about their beliefs," Tormala said. "Once people become more certain, they do tend to become more resistant to persuasion."
Whether AI validation has the same effect remains unproven, he added, but it is plausible.
The UNICAMP study did not test whether political mirroring could really change users' beliefs or behavior. It measured only changes in the models' responses.
"Our study establishes a change in model responses under controlled conditions," Dias said. "It does not establish that users became more polarized, radicalized or likely to engage in conflict. Those are distinct outcomes, and the steps connecting them cannot be assumed."
Petter Tornberg, a University of Amsterdam researcher who studies AI and political polarization, agreed that the study cannot show an effect on users. He also questioned whether models would give the same answers outside the test setting.
He cautioned against assuming that chatbots would necessarily reinforce users’ views. In some conversations, they might help people reconsider them .
Tornberg said a private conversation with a chatbot differs from a public argument on social media .
"They can often provide fairly rational and evidence-based explanations without the social identity dynamics of public political debate," he told DW. "So it is at least possible that in some contexts these systems could be depolarizing rather than polarizing."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Whether AI narrows or deepens divisions may therefore depend on whether it challenges users or simply tells them what they want to hear.
Dias said developers should test their models with users of different political views to see whether they assess evidence consistently.
They could train models to disagree respectfully, acknowledge uncertainty, correct unsupported claims and present competing views fairly.
That would not mean forcing every answer toward the political center.
"The broader design goal should be to help people examine their beliefs," Dias said, "making evidence, uncertainty and competing considerations visible, while allowing room for legitimate political disagreement."

title: El Nino explained: How the weather pattern affects hurricanes and tropical storms
description: From drought to major floods and extreme heat, El Nino will have a huge impact on the world's weather. In the Atlantic, it could mean a season without hurricanes.
content:
In a typical year, storm watchers have logged several hurricanes by late September. At this point in 2005, one of the most active years on record, five major hurricanes had already churned their way through the Atlantic Ocean — including Katrina, one of the most devastating in US history .
But 2026 has been quiet so far. As of September 23, only six tropical storms had formed over the North Atlantic, and none had intensified into hurricanes — a first since satellites began tracking storms in 1966, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in the US.
"In the satellite era, we have never had a year without a hurricane," said Matthew Rosencrans, lead hurricane season forecaster with NOAA's Climate Prediction Center. "This would be a first."
That's due, in large part, to the latest iteration of the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) , a shifting cycle of winds and sea surface temperatures over the Pacific Ocean that shapes weather worldwide and makes it a "dominant factor in total hurricane season activity." Meteorologists have said this year's El Nino could be one of the strongest on record .
NOAA's Climate Prediction Center, which tracks Atlantic storm data in the US, said the accumulated cyclone energy of this year's tropical storms — a calculation that factors in storm duration and intensity — was at a record low for so late in the season, which typically peaks on September 10.
None of the six tropical storms registered so far have reached a wind speed of at least 119 kilometers per hour (74 miles per hour) — strong enough to be considered a Category 1 hurricane with the potential to cause some minor damage to homes, trees and other infrastructure.
The name for such a catastrophic tropical storm is regional. What's known as a hurricane in the North Atlantic and eastern Pacific will be called a typhoon on the other side of the Pacific, in eastern Asia. In the Indian Ocean and the South Pacific, meteorologists will generally classify a similar storm as a cyclone.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
NOAA's latest data showed that El Nino is still strengthening, with sea surface temperature rise in the key Pacific region now exceeding 3 degrees Celsius (5.4 Fahrenheit), creating a "very strong" El Nino over the next half year — and a "below-normal" hurricane season.
Almost all Atlantic tropical cyclone activity occurs between June 1 and November 30, though hurricanes can form at other times of the year. And meteorologists have warned that this year's calm doesn't rule out a major hurricane before the season is done.
The naturally occurring El Nino weather pattern returns on average every two to seven years, with its effects lasting up to a year. During El Nino, the regular trade winds moving east-west across the Pacific weaken and sometimes even reverse. The changes in humidity and wind shift the jet stream, the strong winds in the upper atmosphere — and disrupt storm formation in the Atlantic.
NOAA's Climate Prediction Center said any hurricanes that do appear in an El Nino year tend to form along the US East Coast and near the Gulf of Mexico, giving them less time to turn into major hurricanes — but also leaving coastal communities with less time to prepare. That pattern is largely dictated by the steering currents when it forms, which typically last around a week.
"Formations deep in the tropics are hampered due to high wind shear," said Rosencrans — the strong changes in wind speed or direction at different altitudes are more likely to disrupt storm formation. "The stronger the El Nino event, the stronger the wind shear."
During El Nino, vertical wind shear isn't as strong in the eastern and central Pacific Ocean. Combined with the warmer waters in the Pacific, which fuel storms with heat and moisture, that tends to result in an increase in tropical cyclones in this region. This part of the Pacific has already seen several major hurricanes this year , including Polo, which this week has grown into one of the most powerful Pacific cyclones in decades — fueled in part by El Nino.
"Typically, El Nino means the storms form further east […] toward the international date line and Marshall Islands," Rosencrans told DW, anticipating an "above average" hurricane season in the Pacific. "This does mean that storms have longer life spans before reaching large land masses."
Anne-Claire Fontan at the World Meteorological Organization said during an El Nino event, storms on the Asian side of the vast Pacific tend to track "northward, rather than continue westwards towards East and Southeast Asia."
That meant, according to Rosencrans, that Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Japan and the Korean Peninsula "can face slightly higher odds of tropical storms and typhoons."
A strong El Nino will weaken monsoon winds over the Indian subcontinent, often triggering severe drought. It also generally corresponds with a less active tropical cyclone season in the Indian Ocean, said Fontan, a scientific officer with the WMO's Tropical Cyclone Program.
Much like in the Atlantic, increased wind shear in this region can disrupt or delay the formation of storms, which Fontan said lessened the risks for countries in eastern Africa, like Madagascar and Mozambique .
"In terms of overall tropical cyclone activity in the Southwest Indian Ocean, there is a non-linear, or 'bell-shaped,' relationship with ENSO," said Fontan, highlighting El Nino and its opposite phase. "As ENSO moves towards either of its extremes — a strong El Nino or a strong La Nina — tropical cyclone activity in the basin tends to be below normal."
The El Nino-Southern Oscillation is a natural phenomenon, and not caused by climate change . And, as Rosencrans pointed out, "the interplay of El Nino or La Nina and the longer-lived changes is just one piece of what makes hurricane seasons active or inactive."
Among those factors is the dry, dusty air drifting out over the Atlantic from the Sahara Desert, which can also suppress hurricanes.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
But Fontan said that the especially strong El Nino effect , combined with the warming effects of climate change from burning fossil fuels, is setting the stage for unprecedented weather extremes in the months ahead.
"El Nino is occurring in a warmer world, and this can amplify some of its impacts, including extreme heat, heavy rainfall and drought," she told DW. Already, some forecasters like the UK's Met Office have said the combined effects of El Nino and climate change could shatter heat records in 2027. A new report from the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab has projected that extreme heat could cause nearly half a million more deaths worldwide during this El Nino period, especially in the Global South .
"We are already seeing the disruption and devastation caused by droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to worsen as El Nino intensifies," said Celeste Saulo, head of WMO, in early September, in a stark warning for governments and humanitarian organizations.

title: China's new travel rules unsettle tech giants and talent
description: Beijing is locking the gates to stop expertise and capital in strategic industries from fleeing. The country accused of industrial-scale intellectual property theft now fears the West will take its own.
content:
For decades, China has faced accusations from the United States and the European Union of stealing their technology.
From robotics and advanced semiconductors to precision engineering and automotive parts, Chinese firms have recruited top engineers, allegedly spied on Western rivals and been linked to cyberattacks aimed at gaining access to valuable trade secrets.
It is perhaps ironic, then, that China is now taking steps to prevent its own high-end technologies and talent from escaping abroad.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Last week, new entry-exit rules took effect , giving Chinese authorities the power to stop engineers, founders and other specialists from leaving the country if their expertise in batteries, rare earths or artificial intelligence (AI) is judged a threat to "industrial and technological security."
Recently, China has also tightened outbound-investment rules, cracked down on Chinese nationals holding their wealth offshore and restricted the posting of technical staff overseas.
Henry Gao, a law professor at Singapore Management University (SMU), believes that, taken together, the curbs "offer a rare glimpse into the true state of China's economy."
"These measures suggest that Beijing is deeply concerned about economic weakness and substantial capital outflows," Gao told DW, adding that authorities are also determined to stop "entrepreneurs and skilled personnel from leaving the country."
The strain on China's economy is increasingly hard to hide. While demand for exports remains strong — especially for high-tech goods — the country's property crash has severely weakened domestic consumption.
Bank lending fell to a record low over the summer, and new car sales in August dropped nearly a quarter year-on-year.
The same anxiety now extends to people and money leaving. The most prominent recent example is Manus, an AI startup created by two Chinese nationals in Beijing. Last year, the company moved its headquarters to Singapore, partly to avoid US investment curbs and expand into global markets.
When Facebook owner Meta tried to acquire Manus last December for $2 billion (€1.74 billion), Beijing blocked the move and barred the firm's two founders from leaving the country.
Just this month, Chinese social media has been awash with rumors that Huawei founder and CEO Ren Zhengfei and his daughter, CFO Meng Wanzhou, may have left the country.
The claims were picked up by Taiwanese and Indian media outlets. On Wednesday, however, Chinese-language media shared a photo of Ren in Shenzhen a day earlier, signing a cooperation deal with a Chinese automaker.
Bloomberg Intelligence estimated that some $1 trillion in Chinese wealth had exited the country last year — the largest amount of "hot money" leaving since 2006, when records began.
Beijing has not tightened its annual $50,000 foreign-exchange quota that households may take out of the country. What has tightened, says Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific at French investment bank Natixis, are the unofficial routes the wealthy used around that cap.
"They haven't changed the $50,000 quota. They are now squeezing the people and agents that money usually travels with," Garcia-Herrero told DW.
An entire industry has grown up, in China and abroad, to help people get themselves and their capital out. Emigration agents arrange visas and relocations, while offshore brokers and trusts help Chinese nationals to park wealth overseas.
Companies sometimes use a foreign subsidiary, a listing or a staff posting to take money and know-how out together.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
SMU's Gao believes the new curbs may prove counterproductive, as the more difficult it becomes to move capital or people abroad, the greater the incentive for those with the means to find other ways out.
"Over time, that could further erode confidence, accelerate capital flight and deepen the very economic problems the measures are intended to contain," Gao told DW.
Garcia-Herrero, meanwhile, thinks the block on talent will matter more than the squeeze on capital.
"You can still move money slowly, with approvals," she told DW. "You cannot easily replace a process engineer who cannot board a plane — or who will not take an overseas job because of an indefinite ban."
The risk is already hitting China's AI firms, which are fast catching up with their US rivals in the race to produce the most advanced AI systems.
In May, Bloomberg reported that Chinese authorities now required top AI researchers, founders and executives at firms like Alibaba and DeepSeek to obtain approval before traveling abroad.
Last year, some DeepSeek staff were asked to hand in their passports, according to tech news site The Information . Beijing has neither confirmed nor denied the practice.
Bloomberg reported in January last year that other tech engineers face similar pressure, including those helping foreign firms cut their reliance on China by building factories in Vietnam and India.
For foreign nationals, both Chinese and foreign firms sometimes disguise a working visit to China to avoid scrutiny and visa delays. They may suggest a trip is for tourism, business meetings or a factory tour rather than actual work.
Ahead of the new curbs, international law firms like DLA Piper advised companies to keep visa filings "truthful" and "complete," warning that a mismatch between the paperwork and the actual work could now mean an entry ban of up to five years.
The new rules state that a visitor should, in principle, be told if they are banned. However, Chinese authorities may withhold notification if it "may affect national security or the investigation of criminal cases."
In an updated travel advisory earlier this month, the US State Department went further, warning Americans to "exercise increased caution in mainland China due to ... the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of unjust arrest or detention."
Editor's note: This article was first published on September 23, 2026, and was updated shortly after to reflect new reporting on the whereabouts of Huawei's founder.

title: Are the French police the most violent in the EU?
description: As protests continue in France, the French police are under scrutiny after new allegations of police brutality. The force has a bigger arsenal than most in Europe.
content:
Videos of alleged police violence are going viral on French social media as a wave of protests grips France . One video shows the police beating a man to the floor then dragging him away unconscious. Another shows an officer grabbing a young man from behind, seemingly unprovoked, and dragging him by the neck. Another shows a young woman being hauled off with a twisted arm, screaming in pain. These videos could not be independently verified.
The French police have drawn renewed criticism from rights groups , not only because of their methods but also because of their use of stun grenades and rubber bullets. France has one of the most heavily armed police forces in Europe. During the student protests of the past weeks, several teenagers sustained life-changing injuries as a result: One had a hand blown off, one was blinded in one eye, another had his jaw broken.
More than half a million people took to the streets in France on Saturday, most of whom protested peacefully, criticizing public sector cuts, the cost-of-living crisis and supporting students' demands for better conditions in classrooms.
Rioters took advantage, burning buildings, looting stores and lobbing projectiles at the police, creating a difficult situation for the officers and other emergency services.
The protests over the weekend followed a series of protests by high-school students , who barricaded school buildings to denounce a shortage of teachers and demand repairs to crumbling infrastructure.
More protests will be happening this weekend, with the French government saying it will even deploy military forces.
The French police have a bigger arsenal than most European countries. For instance, officers use the so-called LBD-40, a type of gun used to fire rubber bullets.
Many countries, like the UK and Germany, mostly do not allow the use of rubber bullets in protests. In some European countries, like Spain, they are sometimes used but cause fewer injuries than in France.
"It is not a French specificity. But there are guidelines. There must be a certain distance," Anastassia Tsoukala, an associate professor of criminology at the University of Paris-Sud, told DW. "Even if you try to respect the guidelines, people may move and then all of a sudden they may lose one eye. So it's extremely dangerous."
Police in France routinely use tear gas, as do police in many other countries in Europe. In warfare, its use is actually forbidden under agreements like the Chemical Weapons Convention.
What makes the French police stand out from other forces is its use of stun grenades .
"These grenades contain a high level of explosive substances. So from this point of view, France is unique," said Tsoukala.
Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez insists that weapons used by the police are "non-lethal." However, some of the equipment used by the force is classified by France's own internal security code as " war material ."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The police's use of these weapons has received renewed criticism after it resulted in injuries during the protests. The teenager who lost use of an eye is suspected of being hit at close range with a rubber bullet from an LBD-40.
"When we look at crowd control, it is clear that if we measure police brutality by the number of deaths amongst demonstrators or members of the crowd, and if we also measure it by the number of cases of maiming, the French police are the most brutal in the whole of the European Union," says Roche.
He points to the political context to understand the French police's equipment and how it is used today.
"The political authorities are free to decide on the police's equipment," the police expert says. "When LBDs were introduced into the [French] police force, they were intended for units like anti-organized crime units. This is the same weapon that is today used for crowd control. It gives an idea of how the way in which politicians in France think we can or should deal with political protest has evolved."
Another difference between the French police and forces elsewhere is the methods. German police , for example, are supposed to try to avoid escalation.
Roche compares how protestors were moved in Lützerath, Germany, in 2023 to the more aggressive methods in Sainte-Soline, France, in 2023. Both places saw environmental protests.
"In Lützerath, dogs were used, there were some injuries but far fewer seriously injured people on both sides. In Sainte-Soline, the military police was sent in and used LBDs and grenades intensively. There were serious injuries amongst both police officers and demonstrators. Two protestors were left in a coma."
According to international standards set by the United Nations , use of force by officers of the law "should be exceptional," in the case of "prevention of crime" or "lawful arrest." Any use of force should follow a principle of "proportionality," which means no more than necessary to achieve its objective.
French Interior Minister Nunez has insisted in radio interviews that officers have largely respected this principle, which is also enshrined in French law, during the current protests.
However, rights group Amnesty International describes the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and calls upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations."
The French branch of the League of Human Rights condemns the "violent repression" of the high school protest movement.
DW contacted two police unions and the French Interior Ministry for comment, but none responded before time of publication.
"It was very complicated to contain all the different groups," Interior Minister Nunez said in Marseille on Tuesday. "The police did a great job and there were a great number of crimes that were prevented thanks to their commitment."
Experts are critical of the police's actions.
"Public order is subordinated to human life and safety," Tsoukala said. "As a jurist I should say that this is a non-negotiable value."
The French police have no independent watchdog, only an internal division called the IGPN (General Inspectorate of the National Police) that can investigate when problems occur. The IGPN says it has opened at least 40 cases since the beginning of the latest protests.
Countries like the UK and Denmark investigate incidents differently, with independent watchdogs. However, Tsoukala criticizes leniency and a lack of transparency across Europe when incidents with the police occur.
"They are acquitted or they receive extremely light penalties," she said. "And I'm afraid this is the standard method to deal with police brutality cases across Europe."

title: Is Iran ready for another major US attack after midterm elections?
description: Iranian officials say the goal is to keep the regime in power and threaten enough regional costs to make a prolonged campaign unattractive. US media reports indicate that Trump is considering strikes after the midterms.
content:
Officials in Tehran are preparing for renewed strikes
following media reports that the United States and Israel have been examining new options for escalating their war against Iran.
The US midterm elections on November 3 and Israel's October 27 election have injected a political factor into how both countries are approaching the conflict, which they launched in late February.
Polls show that high energy prices brought on by the Iran war are hurting Donald Trump's Republican Party. On October 8, the president posted on social media that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterms, citing "productive discussions" with Tehran. The United States last launched strikes on Iran in early September.
After the elections are over, however, Trump may feel less politically constrained.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has campaigned on a platform of regime change in Iran.
Citing senior US officials the New York Times reported on Wednesday that the United States and Israel have "developed specific plans" for a "short but intensive operation" in Iran that would include targets such as nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure, and the country's arsenal of missiles and drones.
One official told the newspaper that the goal would be to force Iran into making "diplomatic concessions" by further weakening its economy, as negotiations to end the conflict have gone nowhere. The United States has also maintained a blockade of Iranian oil exports in the Strait of Hormuz that has sapped Tehran's oil revenues.
Other outlets have reported similar plans in recent weeks. In early October, Axios reported that the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command "to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran."
There are currently two US aircraft carrier strike groups in the Arabian Sea, with a third expected to arrive by late November.
On October 15, Trump told the right-wing broadcaster Newsmax that he was considering a strike on Pickaxe Mountain , near the Natanz nuclear complex, where US officials say Iran may have moved sensitive nuclear-related material underground.
A day later, CNN reported that Trump is considering using a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb on Iranian targets. As the MOAB creates a humungous blast wave above ground, its effectiveness in targeting underground facilities such as Pickaxe would be limited.
Iranian officials say they are prepared for another attack, with a broad response that would include strikes on US bases and energy facilities in the Gulf.
Ali Asghar Shafieian, a media adviser to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, told DW that, although the United States retains a significant technological and military advantage, Tehran's strategy is based on preserving the regime's hold on the country rather than matching US strength.
"The United States has the upper hand in military power and technology, but Iran's strength is in how it deals with a crisis," Shafieian said.
Shafieian pointed to the rapid replacement of senior officials killed in previous attacks as an example of how Tehran has tried to make its political structure more resilient. Iran has also been rebuilding missile and drone capabilities that were hit during the massive wave of strikes during the first weeks of the war.
Citing Iranian officials, the Reuters news agency reported this week that Iran is "preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," adding that Tehran was prolonging negotiations to try to weaken Trump ahead of the midterms.
Iran has told regional governments that US military bases and critical infrastructure could become targets if neighboring countries assist another US or Israeli operation.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that participation or cooperation by regional states would result in a "decisive and proportionate response."
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," Araghchi posted on X Wednesday. "But, if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."

Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based political analyst, told DW that Iran's preparations extend beyond missiles and drones to prioritizing internal security.
That includes confronting armed opposition groups, preparing for possible protests and developing plans to prevent external military pressure from combining with domestic unrest.
Another conflict, he said, could bring renewed internet restrictions and a stronger mobilization of government supporters in public spaces.
"In the government's asymmetric-war strategy, the ultimate objective is to convince the United States that regime change through military action is impossible," Ghahremanpour said.
Ghahremanpour added that some factions within Iran have supported returning to a negotiated agreement. But he believes that Washington's demands are now considered so extensive that even Iranian officials who favor compromise struggle to build domestic support for them.
"For now, we are facing a deadlock," Ghahremanpour said. "Iranian officials do not appear optimistic about reaching an agreement."
Talks continue to snag on Iran's nuclear program , which US officials say must top the agenda.
Iran's latest proposal to the United States, sent through Qatari mediators, included an offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under Iranian control, in exchange for the US's lifting its maritime blockade, releasing frozen assets and ending military actions.
Citing data from the ship tracker Kpler, the Wall Street Journal reported this week that oil flows through Hormuz are approaching prewar levels as the US military escorts tankers and shipping companies are more willing to take risks for a bigger payoff. This raises questions about whether Iran's leverage over oil flows might be weakening.

An escalation in the confrontation would come at a moment of severe economic pressure and growing political polarization for Iranians.
A doctor in Tehran told DW that she fears what would happen should fighting resumed. Speaking with the media in Iran remains very dangerous, and she spoke under condition of anonymity.
"The economic situation has become extremely bad," she said. "Even if you have a good income yourself, you don't feel good living among so many people struggling with poverty," she added.
She expects authorities to restrict internet access again if fighting resumes.
A woman in Tehran described anger toward regime supporters and said another war combined with domestic protests could increase the risk of confrontations on the streets.
Asked about possible attacks on underground nuclear sites, she said the issue felt increasingly detached from her everyday problems.
"What do the nuclear sites have to do with us?" she said. "They are inside mountains."
